facts.title: Declining Popularity Declarations (1957-1997)
facts.body: Rock music has been declared "dead" multiple times throughout its history, including in 1957 when Elvis Presley joined the army, in 1970 with The Beatles' breakup, in 1977 due to the rise of disco and ironically the birth of punk, in the early 1980s with the advent of synthesizer bands, in 1989 when it was claimed to have run its course, and in 1997 with the popularity of boy bands, girl singers, and hip hop. In each instance, rock eventually experienced a rebirth. "Rock had been declared dead in 1957 when Elvis went into the army in 1970, when the Beatles broke up."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

facts.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
facts.body: All four members of The Beatles managed to avoid compulsory national service in Britain, which ended in 1957 for those born on or after October 1, 1939, and was completely abolished in November 1960. John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940) were specifically mentioned as being exempt. This allowed them and countless other young British men to dedicate their time to forming bands and playing music, directly contributing to the explosion of the British music scene and the British Invasion. "And in November 1960, when compulsory service ended all together, all four members of the Beatles managed to avoid going into the army."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show – Third Appearance Censorship (January 6, 1957)
facts.body: For his third appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" on January 6, 1957, Elvis Presley was famously filmed and broadcast only from the waist up. This decision was a direct measure taken to appease public and religious groups offended by his previous "swiveling hips." "And that's why, for his third appearance on January 6th, 1957, Elvis was shown only from the waist up."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Lieber & Stoller Collaboration (1957)
facts.body: In 1957, Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller concentrated on working with Elvis Presley, among others, which was considered more lucrative work for the songwriting and production team at the time. facts.title: Relationships with Band Members Strained (1957-1958)
facts.body: Between late 1957 and early 1958, Elvis Presley's personal life and relationships, particularly with his band members Scotty Moore and Bill Black, began to deteriorate. Moore and Black felt increasingly isolated by Colonel Parker and underpaid despite Elvis's immense earnings, leading to significant friction. "In particular, his relationships with everyone involved in his career, everyone except the Colonel, of course, were getting weakened."

facts.title: Band Members' Resignation and Initial Replacements (September 1957)
facts.body: Scotty Moore and Bill Black formally resigned from Elvis's band in September 1957. Their grievances stemmed from being placed on a salary rather than a profit split, a drastically reduced concert schedule (only 14 shows that year), accumulating debt, and Colonel Parker's tight control, which prevented them from even speaking directly with Elvis. Initially incensed, Elvis replaced them for a show in Tupelo, Mississippi, with country session guitarist Hank Garland and bassist Chuck Wigginson. "Elvis was incensed, and decided that he didn't need them anyway."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show – Third Appearance Censorship (January 6, 1957)
facts.body: For his third appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" on January 6, 1957, Elvis Presley was famously filmed and broadcast only from the waist up. This decision was a direct measure taken to appease public and religious groups offended by his previous "swiveling hips." "And that's why, for his third appearance on January 6th, 1957, Elvis was shown only from the waist up."

facts.title: Relationships with Band Members Strained (1957-1958)
facts.body: Between late 1957 and early 1958, Elvis Presley's personal life and relationships, particularly with his band members Scotty Moore and Bill Black, began to deteriorate. Moore and Black felt increasingly isolated by Colonel Parker and underpaid despite Elvis's immense earnings, leading to significant friction. "In particular, his relationships with everyone involved in his career, everyone except the Colonel, of course, were getting weakened."

facts.title: Bob Wills' Definition of Rock and Roll (1957)
facts.body: Bob Wills famously stated in 1957 that what was being called "Rock and Roll" was essentially the same basic rhythm music he and others had been playing since 1928, just under a different name. He emphasized that the rhythm is the most important element, whether accompanied by minimal or many instruments. "Rock and Roll. Why, man, that's the same kind of music we've been playing since 1928."

facts.body: Simon John Richie was born in London on May 10, 1957. He was born without his parents ever being married. "Simon John Richie was born in London on May 10, 1957."

facts.body: Upon learning of Janice Martin's pregnancy in 1957, RCA was furious, believing it incompatible with her "nation's sweetheart" image. facts.title: Crisis of Faith and Music Hiatus (1957)
facts.body: Little Richard, one of the first rock and roll stars and one of the first black rock and roll stars, experienced a crisis of faith in 1957 while in the middle of a tour of Australia. This crisis was triggered by dreaming of his own damnation, which he attributed largely to his closeted gayness. He subsequently quit the music business for five years, and after returning, he never truly regained the level of success and prominence he had enjoyed in the mid-1950s. "dreaming of his own damn nation, much of which had to do with his closeted gainess."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Featured in Rock and Roll Film (1957)
facts.body: Little Richard was featured in the 1957 Alan Fried film, "Mr. Rock and Roll," alongside other rock and roll and R&B stars. This film also notably included Lionel Hampton, the only jazz musician in the lineup, highlighting the cross-genre recognition of pioneers. "You can see him in the 1957 Alan Fried film, Mr. Rock and Roll, playing his vibraphone, as the only jazz musician in a film which otherwise features Little Richard, Clyde McFatter, and other rock and Darwin-based stars at the time."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Religious Conversion Experience (October 1957)
facts.body: While on a tour of Australia in October 1957, Little Richard experienced a profound religious awakening after seeing a plane engine glowing red, convincing him of angels, and then witnessing Russia's Sputnik satellite pass low over Australia like a "fireball," which he interpreted as a divine sign to abandon his sinful life for religion. To prove his sincerity, he threw all his rings into the ocean and abruptly canceled the remaining ten days of the tour to return to the US. "He decided this was a sign, and he was being told by God he needed to give up his life of sin and devote himself to religion."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Plane Crash Death (1957)
facts.body: On February 3, 1957, a day famously known as "the day the music died," Buddy Holly was killed when the small plane he was a passenger in went down in a cornfield outside of Mason City, Iowa. He died alongside fellow musicians Richie Valens and The Big Bopper. "February 3rd, 1957 has gone down in history as the day the music died."

facts.title: Early Career Stagnation (1957)
facts.body: Despite an astonishing outpouring of songs, including "Everyday," "Not Fade Away," and covers of Fats Domino and Little Richard, Holly and The Crickets recorded extensively before having a single hit with "That'll Be the Day" or "Words of Love." "Remember, this was all before they'd had a single hit."

facts.title: Anxiety Over Chart Success (1957)
facts.body: During a fishing holiday in Colorado, Holly was constantly worried about the lack of success of "That'll Be the Day" and obsessed over Paul Anka's number one hit "Diana," feeling his own records were just as good. "But he spent much of the trip worried about the lack of success of that'll be the day, and obsessing over a new record by a new singer, Paul Hanke, that had gone to number one."

facts.title: Racial Ambiguity in Early Success (1957)
facts.body: "That'll Be the Day" gained traction after Black radio stations began playing it, mistaking The Crickets for an earlier Black doo-wop group also called The Crickets. This led to the band being booked on an otherwise all-Black tour without the promoters realizing they were white. "People at Black radio stations had assumed that this new group called the Crickets was the same one."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Harlem Apollo Performance (1957)
facts.body: When The Crickets performed at the notoriously hostile Harlem Apollo, they had to reconfigure their sets because the audience disliked Holly's original material, with the exception of "That'll Be the Day," but responded well to their R&B cover versions like Bo Diddley. They worked hard to win over the audience. "the group had to reconfigure their sets, as the audiences didn't like any of Holly's original material, except that'll be the day."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Dig Records Closure (Post-1957)
facts.body: Johnny Otis's label, Dig Records, closed down shortly after the scandal involving its artist, Little Julian Herrera. Herrera, known to Otis as a Chicano singer and a hero in the LA Chicano community, was revealed to be Ron Gregory, of Jewish and Hungarian American descent from Massachusetts, wanted on rape charges, effectively ending both Herrera's career and the label. "Pretty much the end of Little Julian Herrera's career and indeed shortly after that dig records itself closed down and Otis had no record contract"

facts.title: Signing with Capital Records (1957)
facts.body: After Dig Records closed and Otis was without a contract, comedian Mickey Katz, who was signed to Capital, a major label, saw Otis perform live. Recognizing Otis's talent as a band leader, Katz urged his label to sign him. This led to Otis securing guaranteed major label distribution for his records for the first time in many years. "Cats was on capital, one of the biggest labels in the country and so for the first time in many years Otis had guaranteed major label distribution for his records."

facts.title: Jerry Allison's Drumming Technique on "Peggy Sue" (1957)
facts.body: For "Peggy Sue," drummer Jerry Allison played a fast "paviddle" on his snare drum continuously. Due to the loudness, he had to play in a separate, outside room from the main studio. Producer Norman Petty added an echo chamber effect, flicking the switch on and off to create the illusion of two drummers. "Allison started playing a fast paviddle on his snare drum. Holly decided that they were going to change the tempo of the song, and have Allison play that part all the way through."

facts.title: Nikki Sullivan's Side-lined Role (1957)
facts.body: Nikki Sullivan's rhythm guitar was often deemed unnecessary in The Crickets' songs, and on "Peggy Sue," he ended up not playing guitar at all. Instead, he acted as Holly's "foot pedal," kneeling beside him to flick a pickup switch on Holly's guitar to change its tone for the solo, and then back again. "Nikki Sullivan was already starting to regret joining the cricket, because the rarely wasn't room for his rhythm guitar and most of the songs they were playing."

facts.title: The Apollo Controversy (1957)
facts.body: The Crickets were among the few white acts to play the Harlem Apollo, though not the first (Bobby Darin and possibly Buddy Rich preceded them). They faced a notoriously hostile audience and had to adapt their setlist to include more R&B covers to win over the crowd, as Holly's original material (except "That'll Be the Day") was not well received. "when it reached the Harlem Apollo, which had notoriously hostile audiences, the group had to reconfigure their sets, as the audiences didn't like any of Holly's original material, except that'll be the day."

"And the contract was sent to Jerry Allison, not Buddy Holly. His name wasn't mentioned at first, in case Thiel decided to mention it to his buses, and the whole thing was blown."

facts.body: This song was a big hit for Jerry Lee Lewis. facts.body: This song was immediately recognized as a hit by Lewis and Sam Phillips upon hearing Otis Blackwell's demo. Phillips was concerned about how to improve upon Blackwell's nearly perfect demo. It was tailored specifically for Lewis's established persona, refining the "Whole Lotta Shakin'" formula with a more dynamic, stop-start opening. A film version was quickly cut for "Jamboree," but several days were spent perfecting the hit record, focusing on the intro. Lewis expressed theological concerns about the song sounding "satanic," leading to an angry discussion with Phillips, who eventually persuaded him to continue recording. Released with Hank Williams' "You Win Again" as the B-side, it was an immediate success, selling over a million copies in the first ten days and becoming a classic that defines 1950s Rock and Roll. It established Lewis as one of the genre's greatest stars and has been covered by artists from Dolly Parton to Aerosmith. "It's one of the records that defines 1950s Rock and Roll music, and it firmly established Jerry Lee Lewis as one of the greatest stars of Rock and Roll, if not the greatest."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
facts.body: The end of compulsory national service in Britain in 1957 (for those born after Oct 1, 1939) and its complete abolition in November 1960 meant that young men in bands like The Quarrymen were exempt from military service. This freedom allowed members like John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940), and by implication, all four future Beatles, to continue pursuing music rather than being drafted. "And that meant that the young men in a new group called the Corrie men wouldn't have to worry about going into the army, so they kept at it."

facts.title: The Crickets Naming (1957)
facts.body: Jerry Allison, along with Buddy Holly, decided on "The Crickets" as the band's name after rejecting "The Beetles" as "too creepy." facts.body: Richard Berry's most famous song, which he initially intended to have a Latin feel but altered to straight-ahead R&B at his record label's insistence. Released as the B-side to "You Are My Sunshine" on Flip Records, it became a minor local hit in Los Angeles. facts.body: This song became Jerry Lee Lewis's big hit, having been a highlight of his live show. Its authorship is disputed, with both Dave Curly Williams and Roy Hall (credited as Sonny Day David) claiming to have written it; Big Maybelle originally recorded it with an arrangement by Quincy Jones, and Roy Hall also recorded his own version on Decca. Jerry Lee's inspiration came from Johnny Little John, who performed a faster, lead-vocal version with a spoken section at a gig, which Jerry Lee then adopted for his own performances. Initially, Sam Phillips and Jack Clement doubted the song, thinking it too vulgar for radio and too similar to Elvis, preferring "Middle B. Me" as the A-side. However, after several takes during the recording session, which involved Clement and Phillips contributing ideas, lowering the bass in the mix, and adding slapback echo to the piano, the spontaneous-sounding result convinced everyone it had to be the A-side. "When Jerry Lee took his version of the song into Sun, convinced that this was going to be his big hit and neither Sam Phillips nor Jack Clement believed in it."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Recorded in early 1957 with his backing band, The Upsetters, this song has deep roots, tracing back to "A Bunch of Blues" (1915) and "My Book It's Got A Whole in It," and was heavily influenced by Louis Jordan's version, even including a verse about drinking gin in some takes. The final recording was a "Frankenstein's monster," crafted from a mere 57 seconds of usable material by copy-pasting segments to double its length, resulting in repeated verses and saxophone solos. "So by the time Little Richard came to record Keeper Knockin, in very early 1957, he had a host of different versions he could draw on for inspiration, but what we ended up with is something that's uniquely Little Richard, something that was all together, wilder."

facts.title: 1957 Promotional Film
facts.body: In 1957, RCA issued a promotional film featuring Tchaikovsky's "Romeo and Juliet" to showcase the advancements in electronic recording. The film highlighted how modern technology allowed "great music" to be enjoyed in homes, depicting various listener types ("Smith" characters) who all sought the "truest, most lifelike reproduction of the original music possible," illustrating the era's pursuit of high fidelity. "This is from a promotional film issued by the Recording Corporation of America in 1957. Shh. Listen. Listening to great music, such as Chikowsky's Romeo and Juliet, is always a thrilling experience."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Westrex Breakthrough (1957)

facts.title: True Identity and Career End (Post-1957)
facts.body: Shortly after the success of "Lonely Lonely Night," Little Julian Herrera's true identity was revealed. Police informed Johnny Otis that Herrera, whom Otis knew as a Chicano singer, was actually Ron Gregory, of Jewish ethnicity from a Hungarian American family in Massachusetts, and was wanted on rape charges. Gregory had run away from home to LA, where he was raised by a Mexican American woman. This revelation effectively ended Herrera's music career. "Police came to Otis's door and told him that the person he knew as Julian Herrera was wanted on charges of rape and not only that, his birth name was Ron Gregory and he was of Jewish ethnicity and from a Hungarian American family from Massachusetts."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Little Julian Herrera and the Tigers

facts.title: First American Rock & Roll Group to Tour UK (1957)
facts.body: Bill Haley and the Comets made history in 1957 as the first American rock and roll group to tour the UK. This tour was made possible by the "one-in, one-out" union exchange agreement, which allowed Lonnie Donegan to tour the US simultaneously, this time with permission to play his guitar. "Similarly, when Bill Haley and the Comets became the first American Rock & Roll group to toured the UK, in 1957, Lonnie Donigan was allowed to toured the US again, and this time he could play his guitar."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Bill Haley and the Comets

It has been claimed as the first use of the word "Vocabelli," with Dorsey's son Billy and Johnny's son Rocky cited as the inspiration for the name, though the more likely origin is a portmanteau of "rock" and "hillbilly." "Around this time, they also wrote a song called Vockebelli Boogey which they didn't get to record until 1957. That has been claimed as the first use of the word Vockebelli and Billy Burnett Dorsey's son says they coined the word based on his name and that of Johnny's son, Rucky."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Johnny Little John sang lead on a version of "Whole Lotta Shakin' Going On" that was significantly different from earlier recordings, playing it faster and incorporating a spoken section where he encouraged the audience to "stand in one spot and wiggle around just a little bit." This performance was a direct inspiration for Jerry Lee Lewis's hit version. "Little John singing lead on a version of whole lot of shaken that was very different from either version that had already come out."

facts.body: This song achieved significant commercial success, reaching number 7 on the R&B chart and number 27 on the pop charts. It was recorded in four takes by engineer Bob Sullivan, with Hawkins choosing an early take that captured an audible quick volume adjustment on his vocal. The final version featured James Burton's biting guitar riff and Ronnie Lewis's cowbell-infused drum part, inspired by AJ Tomanello's demo performance. "The song went to number 7 on the R&B chart, and number 27 on the pop charts."

facts.body: This was Jerry Lee Lewis's first really major success, propelling him to the top of the world as the most promising artist in rock and roll music. With Elvis Presley about to be drafted, Lewis intended to take over his mantle as the biggest star. "Holot Shaken was such a massive hit that on the basis of that one record, Jerry Lee was invited to perform his next single in a film called Jamboree."

facts.body: Karl Perkins performed this song in the film "Jamboree." Unlike most of his recordings, this track was not written by him but by Aaron Schroeder. Perkins reportedly found the song "dreck" and considered it only slightly less awful than another option he was given, choosing it over "Great Balls of Fire." He did not believe it was a suitable follow-up to "Whole Lotta Shakin'." "That song was one of the few that Perkins recorded, which wasn't written by him. Instead it was written by Aaron Schroeder."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: Otis Blackwell wrote this song, which became a massive hit for Jerry Lee Lewis. His demo of the song was so impressive that Sam Phillips' main concern was how to improve upon what he considered an already perfect version. "Great Balls of Fire seems to be the first thing to have been tailored, specifically for the persona."
